pr_body:
- Extend search for leading anchor to support alternations.  This means that an expression like `^abc|^def` will now observe the leading `^` whereas previously it didn't.
- Add a FindFirstChar optimization that jumps to the right position for a pattern that matches a computeable max length and ends with an end anchor. For example, with the expression `\d{5}$|\d{5}-\d{4}$`, FindFirstChar will now jump to 10 characters before the end of the input and skip over all match attempts earlier.

Fixes https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/62697
Contributes to https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/64097

issue_context.title: Investigate benefit of computing max regex match length
issue_context.body: Today we compute the minimum length an input is required to be to match an expression; that's then used in a variety of ways,  e.g. checking the input length and failing immediately if we've reached a point where the remaining input is shorter than required. We could also in some situations compute a _maximum_ length.  This could have various benefits, in particular if the expression ends with a $ anchor and isn't anchored at the beginning, if the current positron is less than the max match length from the end,  we can just jump forward to that position, potentially saving on large amounts of unnecessary match attempts. We'd want to investigate how common this is, though, to determine if it's worth the extra compute time.

of course, in a generator, it's "free".

> My assumption was that the analyses we do before kicking off the engine take negligible time - is that not right? would this be especially expensive?

Negligible compared to performing a match many, many times? Yes.  Negligible on the startup path / performing a match once? No.

> of course, in a generator, it's "free".

We can have a higher budget, but it still impacts compilation time, which is something we do care about.

I think it'd be reasonable to add a separate test that validates the FindMode is what we expect it to be for a given pattern, but I think that's separate from this PR.
NIT: since we are visiting every child here, would it be worth to check if each child's lengths is the same, just so that if that's the case we return FindOptimization.TrailingAnchor_FixedLength?
I'm not following. Can you elaborate?

Sure, I'm actually rethinking this and I believe that the scenario I was thinking doesn't really apply and doesn't make sense, but I'll elaborate in what I was thinking anyway just in case. I was thinking of a case where you have a pattern like `((abc$|def$)+)`. In this case, we would compute min length of the node to be 0, and Max length to be 3, so the optimization you made for TrailingAnchor_FixedLength wouldn't be applied. That said, I was wondering if it was valuable to still analyze that for the alternation of the pattern, all branches have the same Length, so I was wondering if we could somehow make this be a sub-case of FixedLength optimization, since if the input is not empty, we can immediately navigate to (input.Length - 3) position in FindFirstChar

> where you have a pattern like `((abc$|def$)+)`. In this case, we would compute min length of the node to be 0, and Max length to be 3

FWIW, we'd actually compute the min to be 3 and the max to be null (unbounded).  It's still the case as you say that TrailingAnchor_FixedLength wouldn't kick in.

It's not clear to me how to reason about an example like you cited.  An end anchor inside of a loop is strange (unless RegexOptions.Multiline is used, in which case it becomes an end-of-line anchor), since an iteration matching means subsequent iterations will fail.  We could thus consider automatically changing `(abc$|def$)+` to just `(abc$|def$)`, since we'll never match more than a single iteration, and then the fixed length optimization would actually kick in, but... this is one of those cases where I don't think it's worth us optimizing in patterns that don't make a lot of sense.  Unless I'm misreading it or misunderstanding it?
I wrote the incorrect loop operator, I meant `(abc$|def$)?` which is why I was saying the min would be 0 and max 3.
NIT: SHould we add a comment here saying that this gets used mainly for TrailingAnchor Alternation's case?

Oh I see, you only save the maximum possible length in the case of trailing anchors and the optimization is to jump to that directly. I wonder if we have considered instead of using a single MaxPossibleLength for this optimization, to use a List/array/collection withall possible starting positions given the diffferent lengths of the alternation, and that might help making FindFirstChar more efficient for some cases where the longest branch isn't the one that should match the input.

Of course, this suggestion doesn't have to be added to the PR, just thinking out loud to see if this is something worth adding later.

> I wonder if we have considered instead of using a single MaxPossibleLength for this optimization, to use a List/array/collection withall possible starting positions given the diffferent lengths of the alternation, and that might help making FindFirstChar more efficient for some cases where the longest branch isn't the one that should match the input.

I don't know that it would help FindFirstChar.  But I did make the computation based off of any RegexNode rather than off of RegexTree with the idea that we could then use it for individual nodes during code generation where it makes sense.  For example, in support of https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/64097, if we're generating code for a top-level alternation like `^something|else$`, we can emit a specialized implementation for it that first processes the first branch, and then if that doesn't match, jumps to four before the end to process the second branch, which we'd compute using ComputeMaxLength on the individual branch.

In case `leading == false`, don't we also want to ensure that all children's length is the same? If not, then I don't think we can make a FindFirstChar optimization to jump to a specific place since there could be different possible starting positions.
As I said here https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/64177#discussion_r791063073 I understand how you handle this now, so you can disregard this one.
